pedagogy.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes the two sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of the equals sign is the foundation: each written line must be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. The persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — are addressed with a balance model, inverse operations, and a substitution check.
bestPractices: Teach 'do the same to both sides' with a balance model so operations that keep the scale level are felt as legal and one-sided moves as illegal.
Insist on ONE valid equality per line — forbid run-on chains like 5−x=6=x=−1; each line must itself be true.
Isolate the unknown with inverse operations; for the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the smaller term from both.
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line / zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; discuss whether an equation has one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
keyRepresentations: Balance scale (unknown-boxes and unit-weights; same action on both pans)
Algebra tiles with zero-pairs for negatives and unknown-on-both-sides
commonMisconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative: 5−x=6 solved as x−5=6 giving x=11.
Considers positive numbers only, so rejects or never reaches a negative solution.
Run-on / operational equals sign: writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then'.
Mishandles the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x): stops at 'unlike terms' or subtracts incorrectly.
Performs an operation on one side only, unbalancing the equation.
Thinks every equation has exactly one solution (misses none/infinitely-many).

learn.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of '=' is the foundation: each written line must itself be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. Target the persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — with a balance model, inverse operations, explicit handling of negatives, and a substitution check back into the original equation.

activities.title: Balance-scale solver: keep both pans level
feedback: If a one-sided action is attempted: the scale tips because the two sides are no longer equal; redo the same action on both pans.

When isolating 8x − 6 = 2x: after removing 2 x-boxes from each side you have 6x − 6 = 0; adding 6 to both sides gives 6x = 6; dividing both sides by 6 gives x = 1. Substitute back: 8(1) − 6 = 2 and 2(1) = 2 — equal, so x = 1 checks.
For 5 − x = 6: using zero-pairs gives −x = 1, so x = −1. Substitute back: 5 − (−1) = 6 — correct; note 5 − x is NOT the same as x − 5.
activities.rationale: 'Do the same to both sides' is a physical intuition made legal-feeling by a balance the learner must keep level; illegal one-sided moves visibly tip it, so the rule is enforced by the model. Dragging actions onto both pans, live tipping, and zero-pair anti-weights are offered as concrete ways to make the balancing mechanism visible; they are examples, not the only possible setup, and are proposed rather than validated as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.
learnerActions: Represent an equation as two pans: unknown-boxes (x) and unit-weights, using 'anti-weights' (zero-pairs) for any negative amount. Set up 8x − 6 = 2x with the −6 shown as six anti-weights on that pan.

Choose an action (add or remove the same number of units, using zero-pairs where a pan has none to remove; remove an x-box; halve everything) and apply it to BOTH pans at once; watch the scale stay level.
Try a one-sided action on purpose and observe that the scale tips — that move is not allowed because it breaks the equality.

Solve 8x − 6 = 2x: remove 2 x-boxes from each pan to reach 6x − 6 = 0, then add 6 units to each pan (cancelling the six anti-weights) to reach 6x = 6, then divide both pans into 6 equal groups (÷6) to reach x = 1.

Use an anti-x-box for −x, plus unit zero-pairs, to model 5 − x = 6: remove 5 units from both pans to reach −x = 1, then swap every item on both pans for its opposite (multiply both sides by −1) to reach x = −1, so the negative solution is something you build and see rather than distrust.
Write down each balanced state as its own line — one true equality per line.
activities.intendedInsight: The only way to keep the scale level while stripping it down to a single x is to mirror every move on both sides — that mirroring IS the solving method, and a negative result is a legitimate, visible outcome.

activities.title: One true equality per line: fix the run-on equals sign
feedback: In 5 − x = 6 = x = −1, the middle '6 = x' is false (6 does not equal −1); the valid working is 5 − x = 6 → −x = 1 → x = −1, one true equality per line.

For 3x − 5 = 2x: subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 5 = 0, then add 5 to both sides to get x = 5. Check: 3(5) − 5 = 10 and 2(5) = 10 — equal, so x = 5. (Note the first item here, 5 − x = 6, has solution x = −1; the two tasks are different equations.)
activities.rationale: The operational (left-to-right 'compute') reading of '=' underlies run-on chains; reading written maths aloud and reformatting into vertical true equalities confronts that reading directly.
sourceClaims: Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.

Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Read aloud, left to right, the chain 5 − x = 6 = x = −1. Decide whether each '=' states a genuine equality (does 6 really equal x?).
Rewrite the working as a vertical chain where every single line is itself true: 5 − x = 6, then −x = 1, then x = −1.
Do the same for 3x − 5 = 2x: rewrite the run-on 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 as separate true lines, subtracting 2x from both sides first (3x − 5 = 2x → x − 5 = 0 → x = 5), and check by substitution.
Spot the invalid line: given a worked solution containing a run-on chain, identify which '=' is false and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: '=' means the two sides have equal value, not 'and then'. Every line of correct working must be a standalone true statement.

activities.title: Solve, then check by substitution; classify how many solutions
feedback: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 expands to 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, true for every x, so infinitely many solutions — an identity, not a single answer.
If substitution does not make both sides equal, the solution is wrong; retrace which line first stopped being a true equality.
activities.rationale: Substitution into the original equation makes correctness self-verifiable and pushes past guess-and-check; the identity 2(x+3)=2x+6 is a concrete counterexample to 'every equation has one solution'.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
KS3 pupils should use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including all forms that require rearrangement.
learnerActions: Solve a set of equations by inverse operations, writing one true equality per line: start with 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x, then extend to equations with brackets and fractional/negative coefficients.
For each solution, substitute it back into the ORIGINAL equation and confirm both sides are equal.
Solve 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 and decide what happens: after expanding the bracket, both sides are identical (2x + 6 = 2x + 6), so every value of x works — infinitely many solutions.
Construct or examine an equation that simplifies to a false statement (e.g. a contradiction) and recognise it has no solution.
Sort equations into 'one solution', 'no solution', 'infinitely many solutions'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solved equation must survive a substitution check in the original; and not every equation has exactly one solution — some have none and some have infinitely many.

activities.title: Sequenced steps and worked-solution annotation (supporting practice)
feedback: 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5); check 3(5) + 5 = 20. ✓
If a line in the annotated solution alters only one side, it is invalid — the equality no longer holds; the matching move must act on both sides.
A static worked solution can display one correct balanced chain, but it does not itself let the learner perform the balancing; pair it with the balance-scale activity where the construction happens.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and fill-in-the-line tasks make the stepwise structure explicit and can surface run-on-equals and one-sided errors through forced choices; annotation of a fixed solution can display a model chain and support recognition/consolidation, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of the balancing moves.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Order the correct solving steps for 3x + 5 = 20 from a scrambled set, stating what is done to both sides at each step.
Fill in each missing line of the working for 8x − 6 = 2x, keeping one true equality per line.
For a step in progress, state what operation should be applied to both sides next.
Examine an annotated worked solution and, line by line, name the inverse operation applied to both sides; then flag any invalid line (e.g. a run-on chain like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1).
activities.intendedInsight: Solving is a reproducible sequence of 'same operation to both sides' moves, and being able to name each inverse operation and reject invalid lines consolidates the procedure.

constraints: Each written line must be a single true equality; forbid run-on chains like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1 or 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 where the '=' means 'and then'.
Every operation must be applied to BOTH sides; operating on one side only unbalances the equation and makes the line false.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line or zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; 5 − x is not the same as x − 5.
On a balance model, represent any negative amount (e.g. the −6 in 8x − 6) with anti-weights (zero-pairs) so the pans and the written equality stay consistent.
For the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the same term from both sides (e.g. subtract 2x from 8x − 6 = 2x to reach 6x − 6 = 0).
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Discuss that an equation may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many (e.g. the identity 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).

A fixed/annotated worked solution and ordering/fill-in tasks support recognition and consolidation but do not elicit the learner's own balancing; they complement, rather than replace, hands-on solving where the learner performs each move.
Prerequisite support for negative-number reasoning and collecting like terms may be needed before equations with negative/fractional coefficients or the unknown on both sides.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the balance-scale approach as uniquely able to 'force' discovery and claims 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' fix the misconceptions. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to a scoped proposal (balance model as a vivid way to make the rule visible) and the static worked solution retained as a consolidation/recognition support rather than dismissed.
The Kieran (1981) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support for the relational-equals principle as unconfirmed here.

Independent self-audit of worked examples: 5 − x = 6 → x = −1 (check 5 − (−1) = 6); 8x − 6 = 2x → x = 1 (check 8 − 6 = 2 = 2); 3x − 5 = 2x → x = 5 (check 10 = 10); 3x + 5 = 20 → x = 5 (check 20 = 20); 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is an identity. The incorrect misconception outputs (x = 11 for 5 − x = 6; the run-on chains) are presented only as errors to confront, never as valid answers.

Balance-scale walkthrough is coherent: after removing 2 x-boxes the state is 6x − 6 = 0, the −6 is modelled with anti-weights so adding 6 units to both pans cancels them to 6x = 6, then ÷6 gives x = 1. Activity 0 feedback was made explicit about the ÷6 step to match the learnerActions and the 'show every line' emphasis.

The diagnostic items 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x are reused across activities as teaching items; they are kept as distinct equations with distinct solutions (−1 and 1) to avoid confusion when both appear in one task.

probeDeeper: Check your answer to (a) by putting it back into 5 − x = 6 — does it work?
In (b), how do you know x = 1 is the ONLY solution and not just A solution? (pushes past guess-and-check)
You wrote 5−x=6=x=−1 — read that out loud left to right. Is 6 really equal to x? (confronts the run-on equals sign)
Here is 2(x+3) = 2x + 6 — solve it. What happens, and what does that tell you about how many solutions it has? (counterexample: an identity / infinitely many solutions)

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats subtraction as commutative / rejects negatives — solves 5−x=6 as if it were x−5=6 to get x=11, or insists 'you can't take x from 5 to make 6' and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute x=11 to show 5−11=−6≠6; rewrite as −x=1 and use a number line to reach x=−1; establish that 5−x is not x−5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes x=11, or abandons the problem as impossible; does not consider a negative solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Run-on / operational equals sign — writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then' rather than 'is equal to'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: One equation per line; read the written maths aloud left-to-right — 'does 6 really equal x?'; rewrite as a vertical chain of true equalities.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A single strung-together line whose equalities are not actually true when read left to right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the unknown on both sides — for 8x−6=2x either stops at 'these aren't like terms' or subtracts wrongly (e.g. treats 8x−6 as 2x).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the balance model to remove 2x from each side, reaching 6x−6=0; then isolate x; check by substitution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not subtract 2x from both sides; leaves the unknown on both sides or mis-collects.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on one side only — changes one side without doing the same to the other, unbalancing the equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance-scale model — every operation must act on both pans or the scale tips; redo the step on both sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A line where one side has been altered (a term added/removed) but the other has not, yet an '=' is kept.

responseLevels.gap: Treats subtraction or sides as swappable (x=11), operates on one side only, or strings steps together with '=' incorrectly; no valid balancing and answers fail a substitution check.
responseLevels.full: Solves equations with the unknown on both sides, negative/fractional coefficients and brackets by doing the same to both sides, writes one valid equality per line, checks by substituting into the original, and can classify an equation as having one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
responseLevels.partial: Solves one- and two-step equations with positive whole-number solutions by inverse operations, but breaks down with negatives, fractional coefficients, brackets, or the unknown on both sides, and may not check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'solve these, showing every line of your working': (a) 5 − x = 6 and (b) 8x − 6 = 2x. Say nothing about method. Watch how they deal with the subtraction and the negative in (a), and how they gather the unknown from both sides in (b), and whether each line is a genuine equality.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items expose different faults on paper without a single question being asked: 5−x=6 catches treating subtraction as commutative (x=11) and refusing negatives; 8x−6=2x catches failure to gather the unknown from both sides and the run-on equals-sign chain. A child who is secure keeps the scale balanced, reaches x=−1 and x=1, and writes one true equality per line.
